Promoting Fundamental British Values

Pupils are encouraged to regard people of all faiths, races and cultures with respect and tolerance and understand that while different people may hold different views about what is ‘right’ and ‘wrong’, all people living in England are subject to its law.

Welcome
Welcome to Moss Hall Nursery School
Moss Hall Nursery School is a long established nursery school in the heart of the West Finchley community. Generations of local families have attended our school. Children are at the heart of all we do and we support them in becoming confident, independent and capable learners.
At Moss Hall Nursery School children:
Like to try new things
Become highly involved in their play
Are intrinsically motivated
Persist when things are tricky
We are a Maintained Nursery School which means:
We are led by a head teacher and employ qualified teachers to lead the curriculum, just like schools in other phases
We give priority in our admissions to vulnerable children and have the skills and expertise to support them successfully.
Like primary and secondary schools, our special needs and disabilities co-ordinator (SENDCo) must be a teacher.
We support a high number of children with SEND and share our expertise in early identification and intervention with other settings.
Our early years practitioners are highly qualified and experienced professionals
We share our expertise with other early education and childcare providers, so that all children in the local community benefit.
We are inspected by Ofsted in exactly the same way as primary and secondary schools (Other nursery providers are not)

Parent Partnership
We believe that parents are the child’s first and most enduring educators and that an effective partnership with parents is of great importance in the early years. We encourage this partnership throughout your child's time in the nursery, starting with a home visit and developing with regular informal meetings and progress reviews. We welcome parents in to work alongside staff in the nursery, for example, reading to children, cooking with children and sharing any particular skills or talents they may have. We organise information workshops and social events on a regular basis. We are always keen to hear parents views on the nursery; do speak to your child’s key person or to the Headteacher, who is usually available at the front door at the beginning of sessions.

What does our local community say about us?
At Moss Hall Nursery School, we are committed to delivering the highest quality provision for our learners, while working in close partnership with families and serving as a beacon of good practice for other Early Years Foundation Stage providers across the borough.
Here are a sample of comments from our community to describe their partnership with us:
“You have been so welcoming, supportive, understanding and kind to this family and it has made all the difference – thank you to you and the whole team.” – Lucy Baker, Lead Advisory Teacher for the Inclusion Advisory Team
“How helpful and wonderful to receive an official lanyard, whistle, staffroom fob and visuals aids. Plus, the booklet about your nursery procedures told me at a glance everything I needed to fulfil my role. I have worked in a number of schools as an agency Early Years Educator role and never has such a warm and informative welcome. Thank you.” – Katherine Forward, Teach Now Agency.
“Our little boy loved this nursery, and so do we. The staff is warm, caring and attentive, providing professional insights on social and cognitive development and scaffolding the children's learning. There is a variety of enrichment activities, and the setting itself is lovely!” - Avital Hahamy, parent of a child in the nursery.
“I just wanted to say thanks so much for feeding back at the meeting today. Your enthusiasm for running the Concept Cat sessions and your experience in supporting the children's language to develop really shone through. At the end of the meeting the other participants said how helpful it had been to hear from you.” - Marie England, Speech and Language Therapist
“Max these resources are brilliant and how supportive they will be for some children. Thank you so much for sharing these with the network” – Joann Moore, Strategic Lead Inclusion Advisory Team/ Head of Service Barnet Early Years SEND Team
“I just wanted to say another big thank you for welcoming us to your Nursery as part of our project. For many, it was the highlight of their day. Max, you did such a great job of sharing your practice and enthusing others.” – Helen Cheung, Strategic Lead for Early Years in Schools
“I am so pleased to hear the great progress (Child) is making, especially around using the core boards to make requests!” – Chloe Laitman, Pathway Lead- Autism and Social Communication
"It was an engaging and interesting workshop. I particularly enjoyed the experience of creating books with my child, with the guidance and input of the facilitator. My child was very proud of her creations, and loved choosing and using the materials provided. The delivery of the workshop was enthusiastic, organised and thoughtful. There were plenty of ideas which could easily be implemented at home." - Priya, Parent from Moss Hall Nursery
"I thoroughly enjoyed my visit to the nursery and was struck by how incredibly welcoming all the staff were from the moment I arrived. The children were highly engaged and motivated, confidently exploring a huge variety of well‑planned activities across the setting. All staff were consistently attentive and fully engaged in supporting children’s learning, development and individual needs. The environment itself was rich, purposeful and thoughtfully designed, offering countless learning opportunities that clearly promote curiosity, independence and inclusion. I particularly enjoyed being part of your Wonder Group session, which was a real pleasure to observe and take part in." - Ruth Vered, Inclusion Advisory Teacher
"The staff members who participated in the adult-child interaction video coaching sessions are continuing to implement these strategies in their everyday interactions, which is reflected by the excellent progress that staff can see the Amber children are making with their language skills within nursery. It is particularly encouraging to see staff consistently reflecting on their approaches and supporting one another in applying these strategies." - Natalie, Speech and Language Therapist (ELSEC Project)
'I recently delivered a twilight training session 'Autism in the Early Years' at Moss Hall Nursery. The nursery SENCO was very proactive in organising this training, and the staff turnout was very high. I found the attendants to be highly engaged; and able to consider how the information delivered fit into their practice. They were very open in discussing children at the setting, asking for advice, and sharing strategies with me and with each other. They were passionate about their work, and highly attuned to the autistic children that they support.' - Jennifer Shill, Autism Advisory Teacher

Childcare Funding Support
Government Childcare Funding
At Moss Hall Nursery, we want every child to have access to high-quality early education. The government offers several childcare funding schemes to help families with the cost of nursery places for children aged 2, 3 and 4 years old.
Below is an overview of the funding options that may be available to your family.
Funding for 2-Year-Olds
Some 2-year-olds can receive 15 hours of funded childcare per week if their family meets certain eligibility criteria. You may qualify if you receive certain benefits, including:
Universal Credit (within the government income threshold)
Income-based Jobseeker’s Allowance
Income-related Employment and Support Allowance
Support through the immigration and asylum system
Children may also qualify if they:
Have an Education, Health and Care Plan (EHCP)
Receive Disability Living Allowance
Are looked after by the local authority or have previously been in care
This funding is available for 15 hours per week for 38 weeks of the year (term time).
Parents must apply through their local council to check eligibility.
30 Hours Funded Childcare for Working Parents (2-Year-Olds)
Eligible working parents may be able to access up to 30 hours of funded childcare per week for their 2-year-old. To qualify, generally:
Parents must be working (or a single working parent in a single-parent household)
Each parent must earn at least the equivalent of 16 hours per week at National Minimum Wage
Each parent must earn less than £100,000 per year
Funding is available for up to 30 hours per week during term time (38 weeks per year).
Parents need to apply through the government childcare service and provide the nursery with their eligibility code.
Funding for 3 and 4 Year Olds
All children in England are entitled to 15 hours of free early education per week from the term after their third birthday.
This funding is available to all families, regardless of income. Children can receive:
38 weeks per year (term time)
30 Hours Extended Funding for Working Parents
Eligible working parents of 3 and 4 year olds may be able to receive 30 hours of funded childcare per week. To qualify:
Parents must be working
Each parent must earn at least 16 hours per week at National Minimum Wage
Each parent must earn less than £100,000 per year
Parents must apply through the government childcare service and provide their eligibility code to the nursery.
If you would like more information about available funding, please follow the link below or if you would like support with the application process, please speak to a member of the Moss Hall Nursery team, who will be happy to help.

Curriculum
According to Ofsted’s Education Inspection Framework, the school curriculum is defined according to its intent, implementation and impact.
Read our statement here:
There is statutory guidance for all early years providers in England which we implement at Moss Hall Nursery School.
Below are some key excerpts from the EYFS document. You can read the whole document at:
Statutory framework for the Early Years Foundation Stage 2025
“There are seven areas of learning and development that must shape educational programmes in early years settings. All areas of learning and development are important and inter-connected.
Three areas are particularly important for building a foundation for igniting children’s curiosity and enthusiasm for learning, forming relationships and thriving.
These are the prime areas:
• communication and language
• physical development
• personal, social and emotional development
Providers must also support children in four specific areas, through which the three prime areas are strengthened and applied. The specific areas are:
• understanding the world
• expressive arts and design
Educational Programmes
Educational programmes must involve activities and experiences for children as set out under each of the areas of learning.
Communication and Language
The development of children’s spoken language underpins all seven areas of learning and development. Children’s back-and-forth interactions from an early age form the foundations for language and cognitive development. The number and quality of the conversations they have with adults and peers throughout the day in a language-rich environment is crucial. By commenting on what children are interested in or doing, and echoing back what they say with new vocabulary added, practitioners will build children's language effectively. Reading frequently to children, and engaging them actively in stories, non-fiction, rhymes and poems, and then providing them with extensive opportunities to use and embed new words in a range of contexts, will give children the opportunity to thrive. Through conversation, story-telling and role play, where children share their ideas with support and modelling from their teacher, and sensitive questioning that invites them to elaborate, children become comfortable using a rich range of vocabulary and language structures.
Personal, Social and Emotional Development
Children’s personal, social and emotional development (PSED) is crucial for children to lead healthy and happy lives, and is fundamental to their cognitive development. Underpinning their personal development are the important attachments that shape their social world. Strong, warm and supportive relationships with adults enable children to learn how to understand their own feelings and those of others. Children should be supported to manage emotions, develop a positive sense of self, set themselves simple goals, have confidence in their own abilities, to persist and wait for what they want and direct attention as necessary. Through adult modelling and guidance, they will learn how to look after their bodies, including healthy eating, and manage personal needs independently. Through supported interaction with other children, they learn how to make good friendships, co-operate and resolve conflicts peaceably. These attributes will provide a secure platform from which children can achieve at school and in later life.
Physical Development
Physical activity is vital in children’s all-round development, enabling them to pursue happy, healthy and active lives. Gross and fine motor experiences develop incrementally throughout early childhood, starting with sensory explorations and the development of a child’s strength, co-ordination and positional awareness through tummy time, crawling and play movement with both objects and adults. By creating games and providing opportunities for play both indoors and outdoors, adults can support children to develop their core strength, stability, balance, spatial awareness, co-ordination and agility. Gross motor skills provide the foundation for developing healthy bodies and social and emotional well-being. Fine motor control and precision helps with hand-eye co-ordination, which is later linked to early literacy. Repeated and varied opportunities to explore and play with small world activities, puzzles, arts and crafts and the practice of using small tools, with feedback and support from adults, allow children to develop proficiency, control and confidence.
It is crucial for children to develop a life-long love of reading. Reading consists of two dimensions: language comprehension and word reading. Language comprehension (necessary for both reading and writing) starts from birth. It only develops when adults talk with children about the world around them and the books (stories and non-fiction) they read with them, and enjoy rhymes, poems and songs together. Skilled word reading, taught later, involves both the speedy working out of the pronunciation of unfamiliar printed words (decoding) and the speedy recognition of familiar printed words. Writing involves transcription (spelling and handwriting) and composition (articulating ideas and structuring them in speech, before writing).
Developing a strong grounding in number is essential so that all children develop the necessary building blocks to excel mathematically. Children should be able to count confidently, develop a deep understanding of the numbers to 10, the relationships between them and the patterns within those numbers. By providing frequent and varied opportunities to build and apply this understanding - such as using manipulatives, including small pebbles and tens frames for organising counting - children will develop a secure base of knowledge and vocabulary from which mastery of mathematics is built. In addition, it is important that the curriculum includes rich opportunities for children to develop their spatial reasoning skills across all areas of mathematics including shape, space and measures. It is important that children develop positive attitudes and interests in mathematics, look for patterns and relationships, spot connections, ‘have a go’ talk to adults and peers about what they notice and not be afraid to make mistakes.
Understanding the World
Understanding the world involves guiding children to make sense of their physical world and their community. The frequency and range of children’s personal experiences increases their knowledge and sense of the world around them – from visiting parks, libraries and museums to meeting important members of society such as police officers, nurses and firefighters. In addition, listening to a broad selection of stories, non-fiction, rhymes and poems will foster their understanding of our culturally, socially, technologically and ecologically diverse world. As well as building important knowledge, this extends their familiarity with words that support understanding across domains. Enriching and widening children’s vocabulary will support later reading comprehension.
Expressive Arts and Design
The development of children’s artistic and cultural awareness supports their imagination and creativity. It is important that children have regular opportunities to engage with the arts, enabling them to explore and play with a wide range of media and materials. The quality and variety of what children see, hear and participate in is crucial for developing their understanding, self-expression, vocabulary and ability to communicate through the arts. The frequency, repetition and depth of their experiences are fundamental to their progress in interpreting and appreciating what they hear, respond to and observe.”
As well as what children learn we are concerned with how they learn. The guidance supports this by identifying three characteristics of effective teaching and learning.
"• playing and exploring - children investigate and experience things, and ‘have a go’
• active learning - children concentrate and keep on trying if they encounter difficulties, and enjoy achievements
• creating and thinking critically - children have and develop their own ideas, make links between ideas, and develop strategies for doing things”
Intent, Implementation and Impact

Introduction to SEND at Moss Hall Nursery School
At Moss Hall Nursery School we actively champion learners with Special Educational Needs & Disabilities. We work closely with families to ensure the child is at the centre of all decisions made to support their learning journey. Our Special Educational Needs Coordinator (SENDCo) Max works closely with Key Workers to identify any specific needs early, then meets with parents / carers alongside Key Workers to discuss any areas of need identified through observations of the child in their familiar environment and formulate a plan for support. We know the Early Years Foundation Stage is a pivotal part of a child's development, and have seen through rigorous study how early intervention is most effective at closing any gaps in knowledge and skills.

Forest School
The Forest School Experience at Moss Hall Nursery School
Moss Hall Nursery is an active participant in the Forest School programme. Over the academic year, we attempt to take all our children out to enjoy learning in a forested area near the school. The aims are for all people taking part, adults and children, to gain a sense of self, to change and adapt, to self-regulate, to build a sense of compassion for each other and the environment as well as develop together as a community.
